# Run Configuration and Orchestration {#sec-run-configuration-and-orchestration}

In [Dash Application Shell](#sec-dash-application-shell) we saw how the Dash app starts, routes between pages and keeps run settings in the browser. The configuration page ends with a **Run Simulation** button, and this chapter follows what happens when it is pressed: how the form values become the parameters the model needs, and how those parameters launch several simulation runs in parallel.

## The use case: one click, several replications {#sec-run-configuration-and-orchestration-use-case}

Suppose a user opens the configuration page and chooses:

- a start date of `2021-01-01`,
- a **simulation duration** of 4 days,
- a **warm-up period** of 1 day,
- 3 runs, and
- the **what-if scenario** switched on.

The form speaks in days and calendar dates. The model speaks in minutes and timestamp strings. Between the click and the first simulated call, three things have to happen:

1. the form values are converted and stored somewhere the model can read them,
2. old output files are cleared away, and
3. one **replication** (an independent run of the model with its own random draws) is started per requested run, spread across the CPU cores.

Three pieces of code share this job, as @fig-run-configuration-and-orchestration-overview shows.

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-run-configuration-and-orchestration-overview
%%| fig-cap: "From the Run button to parallel replications"
flowchart LR
    A["Configuration form"] --> B["configSim<br/>(callbacks.py)"]
    B --> C["prepStartingVars<br/>(oneoneonedes.py)"]
    C --> D["parallelProcess<br/>(oneoneonedes.py)"]
    D --> E["runSim x N<br/>(worker processes)"]
    E --> F["HSM.run()"]
    G["class G<br/>(g.py)"] -. defaults .-> C
    G -. file paths .-> D
```

::: {.callout-note title="In the study"}
Several replications are needed because the model is stochastic: each run draws different random arrivals and journeys. The BMJ Open paper (Pilbery et al., 2023) reports 100 runs of one simulated year, with results given as means and 95% confidence intervals. The form's maxima (100 runs, 365 days) allow that, but the defaults are far smaller. `G` uses 3 runs, and the HSMA talk says its preliminary results came from three runs.
:::

::: {.column-margin}
**Replication**: one complete, independent run of the simulation, identified by its run number (counting from 0). Several are run so that results can be averaged over random variation.
:::

## Global parameters: class `G` {#sec-run-configuration-and-orchestration-g}

`G` in `g.py` is a plain class used as a namespace. Nothing instantiates it: other modules read attributes such as `G.sim_duration` directly. It holds two kinds of thing. First, the defaults for a run.

```{.python filename="g.py:4-20" code-line-style="hi:5-7,hi:17"}
class G:
    call_inter = 0.5            # Call inter-arrival time in minutes
    start_dt = "2021-01-01"

    sim_duration = 5760       # 96 hours 5760 31556952 seconds in a year.
    warm_up_duration = 1440    # 24 hours = 1440
    number_of_runs = 3        # Number of runs
    number_of_gp = 999
    number_of_ed = 999
    number_of_IP = 999
    number_of_111 = 999
    number_of_999 = 999

    prob_callback = 0.5
    prob_male = 0.4

    pt_time_in_sim = 4320 # 4320 for 72 hours
```

Every time value is in **minutes**. `sim_duration` (5760, so 96 hours) is the nominal length of the run. It is added to the warm-up and the follow-up window to set when the clock stops; the arrival generator itself never stops, so callers keep arriving until then (see [Health Service Model](#sec-health-service-model-run)). `warm_up_duration` (1440, so 24 hours) is an initial stretch in which the model runs but records nothing, so that results are not distorted by starting from an empty system. The paper does not describe a warm-up period; it is a feature of this code. `pt_time_in_sim` (4320, so 72 hours) is the follow-up window that each caller is tracked for after their index call. It is a property of the model rather than of the form, so the user cannot change it. The capacity of 999 for each service is effectively unlimited. @sec-health-service-model shows how these become SimPy resources.

The second kind is file paths. Output goes to `data/`, while inputs (observed data and transition tables) live in `csv/`:

```{.python filename="g.py:22-26"}
    all_results_location = 'data/all_results.csv'
    network_graph_location = 'data/network_graph.csv'

    wi_all_results_location = 'data/wi_all_results.csv'
    wi_network_graph_location = 'data/wi_network_graph.csv'
```

The `wi_` prefix marks the what-if outputs, kept in separate files from the baseline so the results page can show them side by side. How rows get into these files is the subject of @sec-simulation-event-log-and-network-data.

::: {.column-margin}
**What-if scenario**: a run in which every caller gets timely GP contact, compared against a baseline run without that change. See @sec-caller-and-call-dispositions.
:::

## From form to model: `configSim` {#sec-run-configuration-and-orchestration-configsim}

The **Run Simulation** button triggers a *long callback*. As @sec-dash-application-shell explained, ordinary Dash callbacks time out on slow work, so long callbacks hand the work to a background manager. Here is the whole function.

```{.python filename="callbacks.py:19-64" code-line-style="hi:20-22,hi:34-39"}
@app.long_callback(
    output = (
        Output('sim_complete', 'value')
    ),
    inputs = (
        Input('run_sim', 'n_clicks'),
        State('sim_duration', 'value'),
        State('warm_up_time', 'value'),
        State('number_of_runs', 'value'),
        State('sim_start_date', 'date'),
        State('what_if_sim_run_value', 'value'),
        State('transition_type_value', 'value'),
        State('ia_time_value', 'value')
    ),
    running = [
        (Output('submit_button', 'style'), HIDE_BUTTON_STYLE, SHOW_BUTTON_STYLE),
        (Output('sim_run_button', 'style'), SHOW_BUTTON_STYLE, HIDE_BUTTON_STYLE),
    ],
    manager = long_callback_manager,
    prevent_initial_call = True
)
def configSim(run_sim, sim_duration, warm_up_time, number_of_runs, sim_start_date, what_if_sim_run, transition_type_value, ia_time_value):
    # Run the sim
    logging.debug("Run the sim")

    global buttonClickCount

    if run_sim > buttonClickCount:
        logging.debug('run_sim > buttonClickCount')
        print('run_sim > buttonClickCount')
        print(f"Sim duration {sim_duration} and warm up {warm_up_time}")
        buttonClickCount = run_sim
        prepStartingVars(
            number_of_runs = number_of_runs,
            warm_up_time = warm_up_time * 1440,
            sim_duration = sim_duration * 1440,
            sim_start_date = f"{sim_start_date} 00:00:00",
            what_if_sim_run = what_if_sim_run,
            transition_type = transition_type_value,
            ia_type = ia_time_value
        )
        parallelProcess()

        return 1
    else:
        return 0
```

A few points are worth noticing.

- Only the button click is an `Input`. Everything else is a `State`, so changing a slider does nothing until **Run Simulation** is pressed.
- The `running` list swaps two buttons while the work is in progress: the Run Simulation button is hidden and a "running" one is shown, then they swap back.
- `buttonClickCount` is a module-level counter meant to ignore callbacks that fire without a new click. Be careful, though: the long callback runs in a separate background process, so its update to the counter is never seen by the main process (which `save_to_local_storage` uses). In practice the test only filters out the initial `n_clicks == 0` call.
- The unit conversion happens here: days become minutes (`* 1440`, since 24 × 60 = 1440), and the date picker's `YYYY-MM-DD` string gets `" 00:00:00"` appended to become a timestamp string.
- The return value, `1`, goes into the `sim_complete` component, which the results page can watch to know the run has finished. Chapters 3 onwards describe what is computed inside `parallelProcess()`.

The `transition_type` and `ia_type` values are the other two form choices. They are passed straight through here and explained in @sec-health-service-model and @sec-transitions-and-time-distributions.

### Saving the same values for the results page

A companion callback, `save_to_local_storage`, runs on the same click and copies the raw form values (days, not minutes) into the `dcc.Store` components from the app shell, so the results page can show the settings that produced the data. See [Dash Application Shell](#sec-dash-application-shell-stores) for its code.


It is a plain `@app.callback`, so it responds immediately, whereas `configSim` may take minutes. When there is no new click it raises `PreventUpdate`, which tells Dash to leave the stores unchanged. Because it is not a long callback, the `buttonClickCount` it sees is the main-process copy, which stays 0.

## Overwriting the model's globals: `prepStartingVars` {#sec-run-configuration-and-orchestration-prep}

The model entry point is `oneoneonedes.py`. At import time it creates module-level variables initialised from `G`:

```{.python filename="oneoneonedes.py:20-26"}
number_of_runs = G.number_of_runs
warm_up_time = G.warm_up_duration
sim_duration = G.sim_duration
sim_start_date = G.start_dt
what_if_sim_run = "No"
transition_type = "qtr"
ia_type = "base"
```

These are the defaults you get if you run the file from the command line. `prepStartingVars` replaces them with the user's choices.

```{.python filename="oneoneonedes.py:51-78" code-line-style="hi:3-12"}
def prepStartingVars(**kwargs):
    logging.debug('Prepping starting vars')
    print('Prepping start vars')
    # Update global variables, not create local version with same name
    global number_of_runs
    global warm_up_time
    global sim_duration
    global sim_start_date
    global what_if_sim_run
    global transition_type
    global ia_type

    for k,v in kwargs.items():
        if k == "number_of_runs":
            number_of_runs = v
        elif k == "warm_up_time":
            warm_up_time = v
        elif k == "sim_duration":
            sim_duration = v
            #print(f"Sim duration in prep starting vars is {sim_duration}")
        elif k == "sim_start_date":
            sim_start_date = v
        elif k == 'what_if_sim_run':
            what_if_sim_run = v
        elif k == 'transition_type':
            transition_type = v
        elif k == 'ia_type':
            ia_type = v
```

The `global` declarations matter: without them, each assignment would create a local variable that vanished on return. The loop accepts any subset of the seven keyword arguments, and ignores unknown keys. Using module globals rather than passing a settings object keeps `parallelProcess()` callable with no arguments, at the cost of hidden state, so it is worth remembering that these globals are the real "current settings".

## Launching the parallel runs {#sec-run-configuration-and-orchestration-parallel}

`parallelProcess` is where the **parallel runs** start. It first clears out last time's output, then maps `runSim` over the run numbers.

```{.python filename="oneoneonedes.py:82-98" code-line-style="hi:8-10,hi:12"}
def parallelProcess(nprocess = mp.cpu_count() - 1):
    logging.debug('Model called')
    global warm_up_time
    global sim_duration
    global what_if_sim_run
    global transition_type
    global ia_type

    file_locs = [G.all_results_location, G.wi_all_results_location, G.network_graph_location, G.wi_network_graph_location]

    [os.remove(x) for x in file_locs if os.path.isfile(x)]

    pool = mp.Pool(processes = nprocess)
    pool.starmap(runSim, zip(list(range(0, number_of_runs)), [number_of_runs] * number_of_runs, [sim_duration] * number_of_runs, [warm_up_time] * number_of_runs, [sim_start_date] * number_of_runs, [what_if_sim_run] * number_of_runs, [transition_type] * number_of_runs, [ia_type] * number_of_runs))

    logging.debug('Reached end of script')
    logging.shutdown()
```

1. The four output files from `G` are deleted if present. This is essential: as @sec-simulation-event-log-and-network-data explains, every replication *appends* to the same files, so stale rows from an earlier run would otherwise be mixed in.
2. A `multiprocessing.Pool` is created with one fewer worker than there are CPU cores, leaving a core free for the web server.
3. `starmap` calls `runSim` once per run number. `zip` pairs each run number with a copy of every other setting, so each call receives its own tuple of eight arguments. `starmap` blocks until every run has finished, which is why `configSim` is a long callback.

If you run `python oneoneonedes.py` directly, the `if __name__ == "__main__"` block at the bottom calls `parallelProcess` with the defaults and no web app involved.

## One replication: `runSim` {#sec-run-configuration-and-orchestration-runsim}

Each worker process runs `runSim`.

```{.python filename="oneoneonedes.py:32-48" code-line-style="hi:7-12"}
def runSim(run, total_runs, sim_duration, warm_up_time, sim_start_date, what_if_sim_run, transition_type, ia_type):
    #print(f"Inside runSim and {sim_start_date} and {what_if_sim_run}")

    start = time.process_time()

    print (f"{current_time()}: Run {run+1} of {total_runs}")
    logging.debug(f"{current_time()}: Run {run+1} of {total_runs}")
    my_111_model = HSM(run, sim_duration, warm_up_time, sim_start_date, what_if_sim_run, transition_type, ia_type)
    my_111_model.run()
    if what_if_sim_run == 'Yes':
        # If what if model running, also need to run it without to generate comparison results
        print("Starting what if is No simulation following Yes")
        my_111_model = HSM(run, sim_duration, warm_up_time, sim_start_date, "No", transition_type, ia_type)
        my_111_model.run()

    print(f'{current_time()}: Run {run+1} took {round((time.process_time() - start)/60, 1)} minutes to run')
    logging.debug(f'{current_time()}: Run {run+1} took {round((time.process_time() - start)/60, 1)} minutes to run')
```

It builds an `HSM` (the health service model, the subject of @sec-health-service-model) with this run's number and settings, then calls `run()`. When the what-if scenario is on, it builds a *second* `HSM` with `"No"` and runs that too, so every what-if run has a baseline to compare against. This matches the paper, which compares the what-if scenario against a baseline (Pilbery et al., 2023). Both use the same `run` number, but they write to different files (the `wi_` ones for the what-if model), so they do not collide.

Note that the baseline is not shared across runs: each replication gets its own baseline model. Timing uses `time.process_time()`, which counts CPU time of the worker rather than wall-clock time.

## Under the hood: the sequence of events {#sec-run-configuration-and-orchestration-sequence}

@fig-run-configuration-and-orchestration-sequence shows the example from the start of the chapter: three runs with the what-if scenario on.

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-run-configuration-and-orchestration-sequence
%%| fig-cap: "What happens when Run is clicked (3 runs, what-if on)"
sequenceDiagram
    participant U as User
    participant CS as configSim
    participant PV as prepStartingVars
    participant PP as parallelProcess
    participant W as Worker pool
    participant HSM as HSM
    U->>CS: click Run Simulation
    CS->>PV: days to minutes, date to timestamp
    PV-->>CS: module globals updated
    CS->>PP: parallelProcess()
    PP->>PP: delete old CSV outputs
    PP->>W: starmap(runSim, runs 0, 1, 2)
    W->>HSM: HSM(what-if Yes).run()
    W->>HSM: HSM(what-if No).run()
    W-->>PP: all runs finished
    PP-->>CS: return
    CS-->>U: sim_complete = 1
```

Each of the three workers does the pair of `HSM` runs for its own run number. They proceed independently, which is why a machine with more cores finishes the same experiment sooner.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Refresher: why module globals and multiprocessing interact carefully"}
`multiprocessing.Pool` starts separate operating-system processes, each with its own copy of module state. That is why `parallelProcess` passes every setting to `runSim` as an argument instead of letting workers read the globals: a worker cannot see changes made to the parent's variables after it was created. Note that the settings are set in the parent *before* the pool is built, and each task carries its own copy of them.

The same separation is why all runs write to shared CSV files by appending, rather than returning data to the parent.
:::

## Conclusion {#sec-run-configuration-and-orchestration-conclusion}

Class `G` provides defaults and file paths, all times in minutes. `configSim` converts the form's days and dates, `prepStartingVars` writes them into the globals of `oneoneonedes.py`, and `parallelProcess` clears old output and fans out one `runSim` per replication, each of which builds an `HSM` (twice, in what-if mode). A companion callback stores the raw form values in the browser for the results page.

Next, in [Health Service Model](#sec-health-service-model), we open up the `HSM` class that `runSim` creates and see how it generates 111 calls over time.
